price.prompt: A purchase price of 150,000 and 25 percent profit. What is the selling price?
price.hint: That 25% rides on top of what he paid; it is not taken off a selling price.

discount.fill: An original price of 500,000 and 30 percent off.

discount.calculateBack: Calculate, and see what price it was discounted from.

original.prompt: A sign says 360,000, after 20% off. What was the price before the discount?
original.hint: 360,000 is what was left after the discount — so it is 80% of the number you are looking for.

realProfit.fill: Reza’s oil: he pays 118,000 and sells at 128,000.
realProfit.nominal: Calculate. This is the paper profit — profit on paper.
realProfit.months: How many months until this money comes back? Tap “3 months”.
realProfit.verdict: Calculate again and look at the real profit.
realProfit.known: Know today’s purchase price? Then no estimate is needed: enter 130,000.
realProfit.again: Calculate once more — now it is working from a real price, not an estimate.

verdict.prompt: The same oil at the same selling price — but this time it sells within one month. Which is true?
verdict.takeaway: The same oil at the same price — only the time until the money comes back changed: a loss over three months, “Thin” over one. And “Thin” is not “Healthy”.
verdict.hint: The only thing that changed is how long the money is away. Over one month there is less price rise to catch up with.

installments.judge: Calculate — Sooda says whether these terms beat a cash sale or fall short of it.
installments.schedule: Open the payment schedule. This is what you send the customer.

monthly.prompt: A cash price of 12,000,000 over six months, nothing down. What is the monthly payment?
monthly.hint: The card showed the “Required markup”. The cash price plus that, split six ways.

verdict.prompt: A flat 2% a month on this deal — how does it compare with a cash sale?
verdict.hint: What it is measured against is cash in hand today, not the price on the sign.

realProfit.a: Paper profit is the selling price minus the purchase price. Real profit is what you actually have left once you have bought the same goods again. In a market where prices keep rising, the two are very different.

rate.q: Where does the price-rise figure come from, and how accurate is it?
rate.a: From three things: the purchase prices you record yourself, how fast your product’s category is rising nationally, and the dollar (if the goods are imported). It is always an estimate, never a certainty — which is why Sooda says “about” everywhere, and why “Why this number?” shows how much of it came from where.

inflation.q: I don’t know the inflation rate. Is that a problem?
inflation.a: No. Sooda has a default rate that comes from the national figures, and you can change it in Settings. And if you know the new purchase price, you don’t need inflation at all: just enter it directly.

data.a: On this phone, and only here. No account, no server, and nothing is sent from your device. The only thing Sooda fetches from the internet is a public rates file from its own site — and you can turn that off in Settings too.

stop.q: Can I leave a lesson halfway through?
stop.a: Yes — tap “Skip” whenever you like. Every lesson runs on a separate practice shop that is deleted when you close it; your own products, history and settings stay exactly as they were.

offline.q: Does it work without the internet?
offline.a: Yes. Install Sooda on your home screen and it opens fully offline. The only thing it fetches is a public rates file, and you can turn that off in Settings.

phone.q: What happens if I change phones?
phone.a: Take a backup file from Settings and restore it on the new phone. Because the data lives on the phone, without a backup it goes when the browser is cleared.

source.a: Yes, completely free and open source, under the MIT licence.

mission.story: Reza bought a shawl for 100,000 toman and wants to make 20% profit.
mission.cost: What he paid goes here. Tap the suggestion and it fills itself.
mission.margin: Good! Now the profit he wants: 20 percent.
mission.calculate: Tap “Calculate”. That is his selling price.
mission.months: Now the real question: what if his money comes back in three months? Tap “3 months”.
mission.again: Calculate again, and see how much of that 20% is really left.
